intro: Five formats you like, turned into formats for your channel: two animation techniques, comics, comedy and an episodic sci-fi series. Borrow the technique, never the characters. Everything here uses your own original characters, names and look.

formats.name: The single-line world
formats.what: The whole world is one continuous drawn line. A character walks along it, the line ends or breaks, and a hand (the animator) steps in to draw what's needed. The character argues back.
whyYou: It's a perfect Delivery Pilot metaphor: the agent walks the line, and the pilot's hand draws the route.
One idea per clip, which is the 'one message' lesson from Inspiration.
Cheap and repeatable: one colour, plain background, no filming. It suits Google Flow or Remotion (SVG path animation).
Explainer Shorts can work (Tokenization Explained: 142 views), and this gives them a recognisable look.
how: Remotion: animate one SVG path with stroke-dashoffset, so the line draws itself
One original character made from the same line (e.g. a small agent with an antenna)
Your hand (or a drawn hand) appears to fix the problem
Mumbled character voice or sound effects, with your voiceover delivering the lesson
30–45s vertical, one concept per clip

examples.title: The 1 Mistake in n8n Loops
examples.beat: The character runs round a loop forever. The hand draws one node, and the loop opens into a straight line.

examples.title: Why Your Cheap Model Gets Lost
examples.beat: The line runs into fog (no context). The hand draws a door labelled MCP, and the character walks through it.

examples.title: Tokens, Explained in One Line
examples.beat: The sentence is a line that breaks into chunks, and the character carries one chunk at a time.

formats.pilot: Make Week 1's 'The 1 Mistake in n8n Loops' Short in this style. It's already in the plan, so it doesn't add to the 3-per-week limit.

formats.name: You + an animated co-host
formats.inspiredBy: Who Framed Roger Rabbit (live action and cartoons sharing the frame)
formats.what: A real person and an animated character in the same shot, reacting to each other. The cartoon is cheeky and fast. The human is the grounded one.
whyYou: It literally shows your thesis, human plus AI agent in one frame: 'AI got CI, humans got delivery.'
It brings energy to talking-head career videos (Pillar 2), the NetworkChuck lesson, without changing who you are.
A recurring character becomes your signature ritual, like the ✈️ pre-flight check.
The co-host can make the mistakes (deploying on Friday, burning tokens), so you can correct them without lecturing.
how: Design one original co-host, e.g. 'Autopilot', a small animated plane/agent, and keep it consistent
Film yourself in the Standup Room with an eyeline mark where the character will be
Add the character in post: Google Flow or Remotion overlay (start with simple 2D stickers)
Give the character 3–5 short moments per video, not a full second presenter
Keep it within the weekly time budget, so add it to videos you're already making

examples.title: Junior Dev Jobs Are Down 50%: Here's the Upswing (re-cut)
examples.beat: Autopilot races through the 5-item CI checklist. You walk through the 5 things that stay human.

examples.title: My AI Agent Tried to Deploy on a Friday
examples.beat: Autopilot hits deploy, you catch it, and the cost meter spikes. Lesson: the pilot owns the release.

examples.title: Frontier-Level AI Coding for Under $10 a Month
examples.beat: Autopilot keeps grabbing the expensive model, and you swap in the cheap one plus LSP glasses.

formats.pilot: Add 3 Autopilot cameos to the next long video you're already making. Don't make a new video for it.

formats.name: Comic-strip explainers
formats.what: A 3–4 panel strip with the setup, the problem, the twist, and a punchline in the last panel. It can be read in 10 seconds and shared everywhere.
whyYou: One idea per strip: a joke that also teaches.
It works across channels: a LinkedIn carousel, a Skool post, or a Short that pans panel by panel. One make, three places.
A recurring original character (e.g. Autopilot) builds recognition across strips.
You can make it without filming, using AI image generation with a consistent character sheet.
how: Write the 4 beats first: setup, problem, twist, punchline
Create an original character sheet once and reuse it in every prompt
Generate the panels (image generation), then add speech bubbles in Canva/Figma
Export a carousel (LinkedIn) and a 9:16 pan-and-zoom Short
Put the real fix or tool in the caption or the last panel

examples.title: The Friday Deploy
examples.beat: Panel 1: 'Ship it?' Panel 2: Autopilot already has. Panel 3: pager goes off. Panel 4: the pilot hits rollback. Who owns the release?

examples.title: Rider, Driver, Pilot (the strip)
examples.beat: Three panels, three seats, and the punchline on who actually lands the plane. It does the job the 12-view Short couldn't.

examples.title: The $200 Bill
examples.beat: An expensive model eats the budget, a cheap model plus LSP glasses does the job, and the Treasurer smiles.

formats.pilot: Turn one planned Short's idea into a 4-panel carousel for LinkedIn (your 30k network). It's the same idea, so there's no extra slot in the video limit.

formats.name: Dev comedy sketches
formats.what: Short sketches where you play more than one role (developer, AI agent, manager) and exaggerate a real dev pain until it's funny, then show the actual fix.
whyYou: Humour is the NetworkChuck lesson: hard material feels light.
Comedy gets shared, which gives Shorts reach they don't get from slogans.
Playing 'the agent' lets you show AI failure modes without preaching.
Your immigrant and career-switcher story has a lot of real, warm comedy in it.
how: Pick a real pain (agent says 'done', it isn't)
Play both roles: a jacket or hat switch, two camera angles
Keep it 30–45s, with the punchline before 0:30
End with the real fix on screen (the tool or setting), which keeps it in Pillar 1
Reuse the Standup Room, so there's no new set

examples.title: Me vs My AI Agent at Code Review
examples.beat: The agent insists the tests pass, you run them and they're all red. Fix: make it run the suite before saying done.

examples.title: The $200 Subscription Intervention
examples.beat: Friends stage an intervention for your AI bill. Reveal: a cheap model in Kilo does the same job.

examples.title: Explaining 'Delivery Pilot' to My Family
examples.beat: Nobody understands your job title. By the end, the pilot metaphor finally lands. Warm, personal, with stakes.

formats.rule: Every sketch ends with something useful. Comedy without a takeaway behaves like a mindset Short (avg 33 views).
formats.pilot: Film one sketch as the Pillar 1 Short already planned for the week, with the fix at the end.

formats.name: The Pilot's Log: an episodic sci-fi series
formats.inspiredBy: Episodic sci-fi series in the Star Trek tradition
formats.what: A recurring ship and crew. Each episode is a self-contained mission that solves one problem, with a log entry to open and a hook to the next mission at the end. Viewers come back for the crew, not just the topic.
whyYou: A series makes people binge and return. Playlists and 'next episode' hooks turn viewers into subscribers.
The cast already exists: the crew are your COBALTS roles (Builder, Operator, Leader, Treasurer, Strategist) as agents, and you're the Delivery Pilot.
Each mission is a real technical problem, so every episode is still Pillar 1 or 2 underneath.
Seasons map onto your Skool course modules: Season 1 = Delivery Pilot Module 1.
how: Original world: name your own ship (e.g. the 'DPV Cobalt') and crew. No Star Trek names, ships, insignia or catchphrases
Opener: 'Pilot's log, sprint 7…' (5s, every episode, your signature)
Mission of the week = one real problem, solved on screen
Scenes from Google Flow plus your voiceover, with the screen recording as the 'bridge console'
End on the lesson and a one-line teaser for the next mission

examples.title: S1E1 · The Token Storm
examples.beat: The Treasurer warns the token budget is burning. The mission: switch to a cheap model plus LSP before the ship stalls.

examples.title: S1E2 · The Silent Loop
examples.beat: The Operator finds a workflow looping in the dark. One node ends it. Teaser: an unknown signal from a new client.

examples.title: S1E3 · First Contact
examples.beat: A new stakeholder hails the ship. The Leader writes the spec (the flight plan) before any agent moves.

formats.pilot: Make S1E1 from the planned '$10/Month Production AI Stack' video. It's the same content, framed as an episode, with the log opener and a teaser.

rules: 🎨 Original characters, names, ships and designs only. No La Linea, Roger Rabbit or Star Trek characters, logos, insignia or catchphrases.
⏱️ Use a format on a video that's already planned. It must not add to the 3-per-week limit.
🧪 Pilot one format at a time, then compare its views with its pillar's average on the What works page.
🔁 Keep a format only if it beats the average twice in a row.
🎯 Every format still has to teach something. A format that's only entertainment performs like a mindset Short.
